content.thinking:
I'm planning the wolf's overall design and proportions for a chunky, hand-painted Blizzard-style model — alert stance, big paws and head, roughly 0.8m at the shoulder and 1.3m body length plus tail, before laying out the skeleton coordinates.

Working out the joint hierarchy next: hips as root, a spine chain curving up through the withers to the neck base, then a neck chain rising to the head, figuring out parenting and joint counts along each catmull-rom path.

Now I'm placing the head and jaw joints, then blocking out the skull geometry: a chunky skull sphere, a tapering snout frustum, and the jaw pieces positioned forward and slightly down from the head joint.

I'm also laying out the tail chain hanging from the hips with three segments curving downward, and starting the front leg joints with shoulders positioned symmetrically and a limb function to define foot targets.

With four points, three segment names give the spans and a fourth adds the tip joint, so I'll name them shoulder, elbow, wrist, paw with paw as the tip, parented to the spine's third joint and assigned a "leg" chain role, using x-position to determine left/right side.

For the hind legs, I'm setting the hip at a scaled position and working out a digitigrade structure — femur angling forward toward the knee, tibia sweeping back to the hock, then a roughly vertical cannon bone down to the paw — checking that segment lengths sum correctly to reach the target foot height and that the hock ends up positioned behind and below the hip.

The paw itself I'm placing as a flattened ellipsoid sitting slightly forward of the ankle joint, with small toe bumps and claws added on top. For limb thickness I'm sweeping a tapered radius along each chain for a chunky-to-slender profile, with a gray-to-cream gradient paint job, and now I'm setting up the body as a loft along the spine path using station points to shape its profile.

Still writing station points...

Writing custom fur paint logic...

I'll make the tufts in 2-3 color variants (dark, mid, cream) using a grayscale texture with a darker tip, so the coat color paint tints them while still carrying the pattern. Then I'll scatter the tufts across the body surface via scatter/cards with varied size, lean, and bend to mimic natural fur flow.

For distribution: I'm planning roughly 260 larger cards on the body, 120 smaller ones for shoulder/chest ruff, plus smaller clusters for neck ring, cheeks, tail, and leg feathering, keeping triangle count manageable since each bent card only costs about 8 tris.

I'm figuring spacing so the body scatter avoids the belly by filtering on surface normal, and setting density so around 300 cards fit the body area without overcrowding. For the ruff, I'm planning a cream-tinted cluster of bigger cards on the chest/neck pointing down-forward with their own spacing and flow direction.

Now I'm working out the throat bib detail: using the surface hit normal to decide which cards get the lighter cream mottled paint versus the darker countershaded tones, applying that filter based on normal y and z so only the lower-front cards get the cream treatment. Next I'm moving on to head details, starting with the skull shape and wide cheek ruffs.

Thinking through how to build the big ears, snout, and nose: I want a rounded chunky snout rather than a flat boxy one, so I'm using a swept rod with elliptical cross-sections tapering from the base to the tip, then painting it with a countershaded mask so the bridge is dark gray and the muzzle sides and underside are cream, like a classic wolf face, with a black nose pad at the tip.

Now I'm working out the jaw and mouth: a lower jaw swept similarly in cream, hinged at a joint near the back of the skull and aimed toward the snout tip, with small white fang cones placed on both the upper snout and lower jaw pointing toward each other so the mouth looks slightly closed, adjusting the vertical positions so the upper and lower pieces overlap just enough without looking broken.

For the mouth line itself I'm adding a thin black polyline rod along each side of the lip from the snout tip back toward the jaw hinge, keeping it subtle rather than fully open. Then I'm placing the nose as a small glossy black sphere right at the snout's tip cap, aligning it with the rounded end of the snout radius.

Now I'm positioning the eyes as amber spheres with slit pupils along the front-side of the skull ellipsoid, checking that their coordinates fall properly within the skull's radii so they sit naturally where the snout blends into the face.

Layering the eye structure now—dark liner sphere behind, amber iris sphere slightly forward, and a small black pupil pushed out further along the outward normal. I'll skip rotation and just rely on scaling for the eye shapes, and I'm considering adding a subtle glow to the amber for that fierce look.

Now I'm working on the ears—extruding a pointed triangular outline, broad at the base and tapering to a sharp tip, tilted outward from the head in profile.

Writing basis vectors and ear geometry...

Finishing the ear outline points, keeping them counter-clockwise with a small bevel and no smoothing, and deciding to skip fur cards for now. I'm planning the cheek ruff as cream-colored cards scattered across the skull surface, filtered by normal direction to target the side-facing regions with a minimum spacing between scatter points.

For the overall coat coloring, I'm setting up a countershading scheme: dark gray on top of the head and back, cream on the cheeks and chin, with a darker mask around the eyes, using a mottled pattern blended between the two tones based on surface normal direction to create that classic wolf face pattern.

Still defining leg paint gradients...

Defining leg radius sweeps...

Adding black claws angled forward-down per toe, keeping the count manageable within the part budget, then double-checking paw placement so the bottom sits just above or barely touching the floor without sinking in.

For the hind legs, I'm working out joint heights: hock sits around y=.29 given segment lengths of .34/.34/.22 from hip to paw, with the knee offset forward using the Pythagorean relation between the hip-to-hock distance and the two thigh/shin segments.

Thinking about the IK direction convention too — for chains with multiple segments, the last bone should align with the root-to-target vector when the hint allows it, so the hock-to-paw direction comes out slightly off-vertical since the target isn't directly below the hip. For hint directions, forward bend at the knee uses a +z hint and backward bend at the hock uses a -z hint, matching how real limbs articulate. Given the complexity, I'm considering whether to just hardcode limb positions manually instead of solving IK.

Setting the hind hip x-offset to .13, just inside the body surface, for chunkier thighs. For the tail I'm building a tapering chain with decreasing radii and a bushy pointed cap, then painting a gradient from the base tail color to a darker tip color along a defined curve of points that sweeps down and back.

For the neck I'm laying out a chain of three points rising from the shoulders up to the head joint, with a wide, ruffed radius profile that tapers slightly toward the head.

I'm checking that the neck's starting radius overlaps smoothly with the last body station so there's no visible gap, and noting the head orientation stays level and alert rather than raised. For coloring, the neck follows the main coat pattern but keeps the cream countershade along the throat to match the belly tone.

Now I'm adding a dorsal mane: dark fur tufts placed along the spine using frames sampled from the body sweep, with cards sized and angled to lean backward for a bristled look, colored in a dark tuft shade. I'm also planning a black saddle marking by darkening the paint across the back region.

For extra detail I'm considering shoulder tufts with scattered fur, but deciding against adding accessories like a collar or bone charm since the creature should stay purely animal. I briefly consider scarring on the flank with slash marks but decide to skip it to keep things simple, and no base platform is needed since it stands directly on the floor.

Now I'm adding chest ruff fur, whisker rods with specific color and placement on each side of the snout, a dark angled brow ridge, and considering a cream chest bib via paint logic tied to position and normal direction.

Adjusting the zigzag edge for the fur boundary using a jagged period pattern, and keeping the painted look soft rather than toon-shaded. I'm staying within the 64 flat color budget since paints don't count toward that limit, and sketching how the tuft texture will render as gray SVG elements.

For the tuft shapes, I'm defining two forms: a broad "tuft" and a thin "wisp," each as a curved path with a white-to-gray gradient fill plus a subtle center stroke line for shading depth. I'm making the tip lighter and the base darker to give each strand a hand-painted, layered feel.

Now I'm figuring out where to scatter these card hits across the creature's body surfaces -- the body sweep, neck sweep, tail sweep, and leg sweeps -- using normal and position filters to target specific areas like the back of the thighs for directional feathering.

Setting up imports and checking the filter signature...

I'll trim out unused imports like stripes and polyline, then define the metadata object with name, description, style, and commit info before setting up color constants.

Defining color palette constants...

Adding bib coloring and coat logic...

Writing face paint logic...

Now I'm thinking through cheek shading — I want cream-colored cheeks blending into the gray face, adjusting the countershade level and softness so the muzzle bridge stays gray while the lower sides turn cream, matching a wolf's natural coloring. Then I start setting up the mesh builder for the gray wolf model.

Building the skeleton hierarchy...

Setting up the tail chain with catmull points, then building a leg loop that mirrors left/right sides using a sign variable, generating front limb points with the limb helper function.

Setting up the hind limb chain with hip, knee, hock, and paw joints, plus naming conventions for both front and hind leg segments per side. Now defining the sweep radii for each leg as tapering arrays so the limbs smoothly narrow from shoulder/hip down to the paw.

For extra muscle shaping, adding small sphere parts rigged to the shoulder and haunch bones to bulk out those areas, then moving on to building the paw geometry attached to each limb's tip joint.

Adding toes and claws...

Still writing body loft...

I'm checking that the bone binding spans correctly cover the segments before the hips joint, confirming the hips JointRef is accepted as a standalone bone reference alongside the spine chain.

Now I'm reconsidering the proportions: a chest width of .35 feels too wide for a wolf's narrower front, and the body height calculation puts the withers too tall if centered at y .81 with a .46 half-height. I'm recalibrating toward a shoulder height around .85, adjusting the hips center to y .70 with h .30 so the back top lands near .85, and working out the chest center position next.

Working out the skull center and radii, then recalculating eye placement relative to the skull surface to make sure the proportions stay within bounds.

Now I'm shaping the snout, defining a radius function that tapers from skull front to nose tip, and checking the overall head length against a wolf's typical proportions to keep it chunky but realistic.

I'm also working out the lower jaw path and its taper so it overlaps the snout correctly for a closed mouth, placing the jaw joint and aim point, then starting on the upper fang geometry.

Realizing the fangs end up mostly hidden inside the closed jaw overlap, so I'm considering posing the jaw open by a few degrees to make them visible.

I'm also planning a small pink tongue ellipsoid attached to the jaw bone, but checking its placement so it doesn't get swallowed inside the jaw volume -- nudging the y-position upward so it actually pokes out.

For the nose, I'm placing a dark nose pad sphere near the snout tip with a tiny glossy white highlight sphere for a Blizzard-style shine, skipping nostril details for simplicity. Now I'm figuring out the ear base position relative to the skull's top-back-side.

Still refining ear geometry...

For the inner ear texture I'm using a mottled cream color with a fluffy paint effect, and setting up the ear paint function so the tip area turns black while the base stays dark. I'm also working out the tilt vectors so the ears angle outward symmetrically on each side, checking the dot product to confirm the axes stay orthogonal.

Checking cross product orientation for the mirrored side...

That gives the wrong face direction, so I'm fixing it by keeping the thickness axis pointed consistently toward +Z regardless of mirroring, adjusting the x/y basis vectors so the cross product stays positive even for the mirrored ear, accepting a slight asymmetry rather than flipping the whole outline.

Now I'm skipping back-ear tufts and setting up cheek ruff cards: scattering tuft points across the skull surface filtered by position and normal angle, then laying down tuft-wisp cards with lean, bend, and flow parameters to simulate directional fur.

Adding brow and crown dark tufts with similar scatter logic, then moving to the body surface to scatter a larger set of fur cards there too.

Adding ruff cards for neck/chest fur, verifying the cream bib coloring aligns with the neck z-range, then adding a separate chest ruff patch filtered by forward-facing normals, and starting on dorsal ridge frames along the body spine.

For the neck mane I'll sweep along t from .1 to .95 with 12 frames, steeper lean, darker color, and bigger cards. Tail cards get a surface scatter with downward-back flow and tail paint color, and for leg feathering I'm filtering scatter points by normal and height to isolate the back-of-leg region on front legs.

Legs all use a shared leg scatter with downward flow and gradient coloring from legBase across front and hind, rather than separate paints, since the difference is minor. Then I'm setting the jaw pose rotation, noting that positive degrees tip a forward-pointing bone downward.

I want to add some decorative detail too — a small tribal necklace with a fang pendant and beads, looping a cord around the neck joint for a cute hero-asset touch.

Actually, pinpointing the exact front-facing position for a hanging pendant is too fiddly and risks errors, so I'll skip the necklace entirely. It's safer to keep the design simpler rather than chase an uncertain accessory placement.

Instead, a small gold ring piercing on the left ear could work as a subtle accessory, computing its position by projecting outward from the ear's local coordinates with an outward tilt, then placing the torus ring flat in its default orientation.

Then I'm checking floor contact for the paws and toe placement, scattering some texture detail across the skull surface, and setting up the dx/z offsets for each toe to vary their spacing and depth slightly.

Checking the spike helper signature for claws, confirming limb paths return vectors compatible with chain input, and verifying part/color typing and paint callback parameter usage across coat, face, and ear functions to avoid unused-param errors.

Now I'm sketching tuft SVG shapes with gradient fills and stroke outlines for grass-like tufts, adjusting curve paths for variation between tuftA and tuftB.

Then I shift to the tail's coat coloring, applying mottled countershading gradients to build a base paint layer for the tail texture.

Writing sweep parameters for neck, tail, and legs...

Now I'm setting up the eye geometry, mirroring left and right using a sign multiplier, placing black sclera, glowing iris, and pupil spheres positioned on the head bone.

I realize the pupil sits slightly inside the amber iris surface, so I need to push its z-position forward to keep it visible. Then I'm planning the brow shape as a swept dark line following angled points above each eye, giving the face an angry slant with the inner brow lower than the outer.

Writing whisker and mouth sweeps...

Now I'm adding mottled cream shading for the jaw and chin, applying face paint for the upper snout, and setting up the spine chain with hips as parent before finalizing the file.
